fields.title: What events do to analytics
fields.keyTakeaway: Technical events are accurate and show only successful outcomes, so product behavior is measured separately, and technical event structure must not be dictated by report needs.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: If the system already publishes events for every action, why do we need separate product analytics?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The temptation to use technical events as product events is great: they already exist, they are accurate, they require no client-side work. Products that yield to it find out a year later that metrics cannot be changed without affecting system operations, and half of product questions cannot be answered.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Technical and product events answer different questions.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: *Technical event* — what happened in the system: `order.created`, `payment.confirmed`. Accurate, reliable, comes from the server, independent of the client.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: *Product event* — what a person did: opened a screen, scrolled a feed, cancelled midway, left without finishing. Most of this **leaves no trace in the system at all** because it changed nothing.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Hence the main limitation: **technical events only show what succeeded.** Orders that were placed. Drop-offs, doubts, attempts, back-clicks are invisible — exactly what a PM cares about.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: What you should take from technical events: facts where accuracy matters and discrepancies are unacceptable. Number of orders, amounts, statuses. This is more reliable than client-side analytics, which loses data due to network issues and ad blockers.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: What you shouldn't: behavior. It is measured on the client.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *Do not change technical events for analytics.* As soon as event structure starts being dictated by reports, changing a report becomes changing the system. *Cross-check one against the other.* `order.created` count versus checkout product events — that exact reconciliation from `DS3-N4-L2` that catches event loss in a mobile app.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *From technical events:* orders, revenue, statuses, cancellations, accruals. Everything that goes into partner reports and finance.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *From client analytics:* checkout funnel, drop-offs, filter usage, catalog browsing depth.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: The case that defined the rule: marketing asked to add traffic source to `order.created` to calculate channel conversion. We refused — the event describes the order, not the user's path to it. Traffic source went into client analytics and links to the order via an identifier.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Half a year later, traffic sources were restructured three times. Each restructuring would have been a change to the event structure that nine handlers depended on.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: For a small product, separation is overkill: while there are a dozen events, they can cover both. Separation is worth it when events have more than two subscribers.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Technical events are accurate and show only successful outcomes, so product behavior is measured separately, and technical event structure must not be dictated by report needs.
